Our Loft Conversion Services in London

Every London house is different, from Victorian terraces with back additions to 1930s semis with hipped roofs. Choose a conversion type to see how it works, what it costs and whether it suits your home.

Dormer Loft Conversion

A box extension off the rear roof slope that adds full-height floor space. The most common loft conversion in London.

Hip-to-Gable Loft Conversion

Straightens a sloping side roof into a vertical gable wall, ideal for semi-detached and end-of-terrace houses.

Mansard Loft Conversion

Rebuilds the roof with near-vertical sides for the most space possible. A classic on London terraced streets.

Velux Loft Conversion

Rooflight windows fitted into the existing roof slope. The quickest and simplest conversion where headroom allows.

The problems a loft solves

What Problems Does a London Loft Conversion Fix?

Most people call us because the house has stopped working for them, not because they want a building project. These are the problems we solve most often.

Not enough bedrooms

A growing family is the most common reason to convert. A loft can add a double bedroom, often with an en-suite, on a floor of its own, so the original bedrooms below stay as they are and nobody has to share. It is usually the simplest way to go from two bedrooms to three, or three to four, without losing any garden.

13%: the value an extra double bedroom adds to a typical two-bedroom house, according to Nationwide's 2025 research.1

Nowhere quiet to work

Working from a kitchen table or a spare corner wears thin quickly. A loft office sits above the noise of the house, gets good daylight from rooflights or a dormer window, and can be wired with proper data and power from the start. When the working day ends, you close the door on it.

Planning tip: a home office in the loft is a normal part of a house, so it does not need any change of use.

A loft that looks too low

Plenty of London lofts look too cramped at first glance. A dormer adds full-height space at the rear, a mansard lifts the whole back slope, and in some houses the ceilings below can be lowered. We measure the head height at the free survey and tell you honestly what is possible.

2 metres: the headroom Building Regulations require over a new loft staircase, reducing to 1.9 m in the middle and 1.8 m at the side under a sloping roof.2

Moving costs too much

Buying a bigger house in London means stamp duty, agents' fees, removal costs and often a longer commute or a new school. Adding the space where you already live keeps your neighbours, schools and transport links, and the money goes into your own property instead of fees.

5%: the price increase Nationwide found for every 10% of extra floor space added to a typical house.1

A cold, unused roof space

An unconverted loft is often the least insulated part of the house. Converting it means the new roof is insulated to modern standards, so the loft room stays warm in winter and the bedrooms below stop losing heat through the ceiling.

0.15 W/m²K: the maximum heat loss (U-value) Building Regulations allow for a new roof element in an existing home.3

Worries about fire safety on three floors

Adding a third storey changes how you would leave the house in a fire. We design the escape route in from day one: a protected staircase down to the front door, fire-resisting doors onto it, and mains-powered smoke alarms linked together on every floor.

Approved Document B: the part of the Building Regulations that building control checks before signing off a new loft storey.4

Choosing the right loft

What Types of Loft Conversion Do We Offer in London?

The right conversion depends on your roof shape, your street and how much space you need. Here is how the main options compare.

Rear dormer loft conversions

A rear dormer extends vertically out of the back roof slope to create a flat-roofed room with full standing height. It suits most terraced, semi-detached and detached houses, and the front of the house stays unchanged from the street. Because it does not alter the front roof slope, a rear dormer is often permitted development, which avoids a full planning application.

40 m³ / 50 m³: the extra roof volume permitted development allows on a terraced house and on other houses.5

Hip-to-gable loft conversions

Many 1930s London semis have a hipped roof that slopes down at the side, leaving a narrow, awkward loft. A hip-to-gable conversion builds the side wall straight up to the ridge, which creates room for the staircase to land comfortably. It is often combined with a rear dormer for the most usable floor area.

6 to 8 weeks: the typical build time for a hip-to-gable conversion, once design and approvals are in place.6

Mansard loft conversions

A mansard replaces the rear roof slope with a near-vertical wall at about 72 degrees, with windows set into small dormers. It gives the most floor space of any loft conversion and is a familiar sight on London terraced streets, which is why many councils accept it. It almost always needs full planning permission.

12 to 16 weeks: the typical build time for a mansard, the longest of the main loft types.7

Velux and rooflight loft conversions

If your loft already has enough head height, a rooflight conversion keeps the roof shape exactly as it is and simply adds windows in the slope, insulation, flooring and a staircase. There is less structural work, so it is usually the quickest and lowest-cost loft conversion.

150 mm: the most a rooflight can project above the roof slope and still count as permitted development.5

L-shaped dormer conversions

Victorian and Edwardian terraces often have a back addition, or outrigger, with its own lower roof. An L-shaped dormer joins a dormer on the main roof with a second dormer over the outrigger, forming an L. The result is usually enough space for two bedrooms, or a bedroom and a bathroom.

2 months: the minimum party wall notice before cutting into a shared wall, which most L-shaped conversions on terraces do.8

Loft bathrooms and en-suites

Adding a bathroom alongside a new loft bedroom makes the top floor a self-contained suite, which is what buyers look for. We plan the drainage route, ventilation and waterproofing as part of the structural design, so the bathroom fits under the roof without any compromises later.

Up to 24%: the value Nationwide found a large bedroom plus bathroom can add to a home.1

How it works

Your London Loft Conversion, Step by Step

  1. Free survey

    We visit, measure the loft and roof, check head height and talk through how you want to use the space.

  2. Design and approvals

    Drawings, structural calculations, planning or a lawful development certificate, and party wall notices.

  3. The build

    Scaffolding goes up, the roof and floor are built from outside, and the staircase goes in near the end.

  4. Sign-off and handover

    Building control's final inspection, your completion certificate, and a finished room ready to use.

FAQ

Loft Conversion Questions We Get Asked Most

Do I need planning permission for a loft conversion in London?

Many London loft conversions are permitted development, which means no planning application is needed, as long as the extra roof space is under 40 cubic metres for a terraced house or 50 cubic metres for other houses, nothing rises above the existing ridge and the front roof slope facing the road is left unchanged. Mansards, flats, conservation areas and streets with an Article 4 direction usually need full planning permission. We check your property at the free survey and tell you which route applies.

How much does a loft conversion cost in London?

Published London price guides put a rear dormer at roughly £40,000 to £90,000, a hip-to-gable at roughly £52,000 to £69,000 and a mansard at roughly £55,000 to £90,000. The final figure depends on the size of the loft, the roof structure, the staircase position, the finish and whether you add a bathroom. You get a fixed written quote after the free survey.

How long does a loft conversion take?

A dormer or hip-to-gable loft conversion typically takes 6 to 8 weeks on site, and a mansard typically takes 12 to 16 weeks. Planning, party wall notices and structural design come before the build starts, so allow extra time for those.

Can we stay in the house during the work?

Yes, most families stay at home. The majority of the work happens from scaffolding outside, and the loft is only opened up to the rest of the house near the end, when the new staircase goes in.

Do I need a party wall agreement for a loft conversion?

If you live in a terraced or semi-detached house and the work involves cutting into the shared wall, for example to support new steel beams, the Party Wall etc. Act 1996 requires you to give your neighbours at least two months' written notice before that work starts. We help you prepare and serve the notices.

How much head height do I need for a loft conversion?

A height of about 2.2 metres from the top of the ceiling joists to the underside of the ridge is a common rule of thumb for a comfortable loft room. If your loft is lower, a dormer, a mansard or lowering the ceilings below can often create the space. Building Regulations also set a minimum of 2 metres of headroom over a new loft staircase, which can reduce to 1.9 metres in the middle of the stair and 1.8 metres at the side where the roof slopes.

How much value does a loft conversion add?

Nationwide's 2025 research found that adding a double bedroom and bathroom through an extension or loft conversion can add up to 24% to a home's value, and that an extra double bedroom alone adds around 13% to a typical two-bedroom house. The actual uplift depends on your street and the quality of the finish.

What fire safety rules apply when the house becomes three storeys?

Under Building Regulations Approved Document B, a new loft storey needs a safe escape route. That usually means a protected staircase from the loft to the front door with fire-resisting doors onto it, plus mains-powered, interlinked smoke alarms on every floor. Building control checks this before signing the loft off.
